explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Paul says, "All of these must be done to build up the church." Every psalm, teaching and tongue is there for the people in the room. It's like a cookie box: the cookies aren't there to look good, they're there for whoever opens the lid.

Paul doesn't say one word about honoring anybody in this verse. What he says is that all of it must be done "…to build up the church." Paul is an apostle himself (1 Corinthians 1:1), and the goal he names isn't applause for him or anyone else. The goal is the church getting built up, baker.

Nice guess, but Paul never says that here. He lists what people bring, a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue or an interpretation. Then he gives the one job for all of it: "…to build up the church." The target is the church, not proving anything.

Yep. Paul says two or at most three should speak in turn, "…and someone must interpret." (1 Corinthians 14:27) Taking turns plus an interpreter is the whole setup, baker. And if there's no interpreter, he says the speaker should remain silent in the church and speak only to himself and God (1 Corinthians 14:28).

Paul doesn't ask for kneeling anywhere in these verses. His rule for tongues is turns, two or at most three speakers, and then "…someone must interpret." My knees are glad, because I'm standing on a gold base and kneeling would be a whole production. The interpreter is the piece he adds.
No elder shows up in this verse, friend. Paul doesn't ask for an approval stamp. And I know stamps. He says speakers go in turn, "…and someone must interpret."

True. Paul says if there is no interpreter, "…he should remain silent in the church…" He isn't told to stop for good, though. He can "…speak only to himself and God." The church part waits for an interpreter.

It's actually true, friend. Paul says, "But if there is no interpreter, he should remain silent in the church…" So without an interpreter, the one with a tongue stays quiet in the church. He can still speak only to himself and God. That's the plan Paul gives.

True! Paul says, "Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should weigh carefully what is said." So the listeners have a job too, and it isn't just sitting there nodding. Listening with your whole brain counts as work, baker. I can't even listen to my own timer that closely.

This one is true, friend. Paul says, "Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should weigh carefully what is said." The others don't just sit back. They weigh what they hear. Careful listening is part of the meeting.

Right. Paul says, "And if a revelation comes to someone who is seated, the first speaker should stop." The speaker makes room for the new word. Picture me with a stamp mid-press and somebody yelling "hold up!" I'd lift that mustache so fast.
Close, but Paul flips it. He says the first speaker is the one who should stop. The seated person is the one who received the new revelation. So the first speaker makes room, baker.

Nope, friend, and your ears can be glad about it. Paul says the first speaker "should stop." Two people talking at once is exactly what these rules are steering away from. In his words, "…you can all prophesy in turn…" (1 Corinthians 14:31).
That's the reason. Paul says they can all prophesy in turn "…so that everyone may be instructed and encouraged." Turns open the door for everyone to be instructed and encouraged, baker.

explanations.answer: So the leaders stay in charge
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. He says they can all prophesy, and he gives the reason: "…so that everyone may be instructed and encouraged." The verse is about everyone being helped. Leaders staying in charge isn't in it, baker.

explanations.answer: So the meeting ends on time
explanations.explanation: Paul never mentions a clock, friend, and believe me I'd have noticed. The reason he gives is "…so that everyone may be instructed and encouraged." It's about people being taught and lifted up. A clock isn't in the picture.

Yes! Paul says, "For God is not a God of disorder, but of peace…" That's the reason behind the turns, the interpreter and the stopping. The rules aren't there to squash anybody. They match who God is, baker.

Good word, but it's not the one Paul uses here. He sets disorder next to peace: "…God is not a God of disorder, but of peace…" That's the reason he gives for the order he asks them to follow, turns instead of everybody at once. Peace is the word he picks.
Not this time, friend. Paul says God is "…not a God of disorder, but of peace…" Judgment isn't in the verse at all. The turns and the order he asks for sit under the word peace.

Close, but it's false. Paul keeps going right after "peace" and says, "…as in all the churches of the saints." So he isn't just talking about Corinth. He ties their meeting to the other churches too. One line later, and the picture gets way bigger.

False is right. After calling God a God of peace, Paul adds, "…as in all the churches of the saints." So Corinth isn't the only church in view. He points to all the churches. That's a lot of meetings to keep peaceful, baker.
That's the one. Paul says women "…must be in submission, as the law says." He names the law, and the verse doesn't point to a specific passage in it. So I'll stay right where the text stays, friend.

Paul doesn't point to the prophets in this verse. He says women "…must be in submission, as the law says." Prophets do show up earlier in the passage, speaking in turn, but they aren't what he points to here. The word he uses is the law, baker.
No elders in this verse, friend. I checked twice, and the one thing Paul points to is the law. He writes that women "…must be in submission, as the law says."

True. Paul says, "If anyone considers himself a prophet or spiritual person, let him acknowledge that what I am writing you is the Lord’s command." He's talking to people who see themselves as spiritual. Those are the very people he asks to acknowledge it, baker.

This one is true, friend. Paul says, "If anyone considers himself a prophet or spiritual person, let him acknowledge that what I am writing you is the Lord’s command." So the people who think they're prophets or spiritual are the ones he's talking to. He asks them to acknowledge it.

Yes. Paul says, "But if anyone ignores this, he himself will be ignored." Hear how the words echo each other, ignores and ignored? Paul stops there. He doesn't say who will do the ignoring or spell out more.
Paul doesn't say that, friend. His words are, "But if anyone ignores this, he himself will be ignored." Nothing about leaving the church is in the verse. I'll stick to what he wrote.

Paul never says that here, baker. What he writes is, "But if anyone ignores this, he himself will be ignored." Losing a gift isn't in that verse, and I'm not adding sprinkles the recipe never called for.

That's it! Paul says, "So, my brothers, be eager to prophesy…" After all the rules, he doesn't just say hush. He tells them to be eager. That's a whole lot of excitement for a letter about turns, friend.
Teaching is on Paul's list earlier, but it isn't what he says here. His wrap-up is "…be eager to prophesy…" That's the one he highlights. Good guess though, baker.
Healing isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage, friend. Paul's wrap-up line is "…be eager to prophesy…" So that's the word that goes in the blank. I can't stamp a heal in there.
It's actually the other way around. Paul says, "…do not forbid speaking in tongues." So he tells them not to forbid it. After all those rules, he still leaves the door open, baker.
False is right. Paul says, "…do not forbid speaking in tongues." So the turns and the interpreter don't mean tongues get banned. He tells them not to forbid it, friend.

You got it, baker. Paul closes with, "But everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner." It's the same thought as God not being a God of disorder (1 Corinthians 14:33). Everything in the meeting gets done that way, and Paul ends on it.
Those are lovely words, but they aren't Paul's. His last line says everything must be done "…in a proper and orderly manner." Order is the word he lands on. Good thought though, friend.
Not quite, baker. Paul's closing line is that everything must be done "…in a proper and orderly manner." Bold and simple don't show up in it. Order is what he finishes with.
